title: Ask about the light, not the caste
hook: recognize the light in everyone and do not ask their caste (Asa, ang 349)

segments.voice: Yesterday, from woman we are born. Your line was why call her lesser. Did you thank a woman out loud? Today, another label the Gurus refused to use. Day two hundred forty-eight.
screen: `FROM WOMAN WE ARE BORN — WHY CALL HER LESSER.`

segments.voice: You meet someone new. Within about a minute, most of us are quietly sorting: where are you from, what do you do, where did you go to school, what's your last name. We don't always mean harm by it. It's how people have measured each other for a very long time. In Guru Nanak's world, the big sorting question was caste, the group you were born into, which could decide whom you ate with, whom you married, even whether you could enter a temple. Guru Nanak had a one-line answer. Today: ask about the light.
screen: `THE FIRST MINUTE: SORTING.` → `WHERE, WHAT, WHICH NAME?` → `THE BIG QUESTION THEN: CASTE.`

segments.voice: On Ang 349, in Rag Asa, Guru Nanak sings: jaanahu jot na poochhahu jaatee aagai jaat na he. Recognize the light, don't ask about caste; in the world beyond, there is no caste. Two words carry it. Jot is light, the divine light Sikhs believe shines in every person. Jaat is caste, birth-group. And the verbs are the point: jaanahu, know, recognize. Na poochhahu, don't even ask. Guru Nanak isn't only saying caste doesn't matter to God. He's saying don't make it the first question you put to a human being. The Gurus didn't leave this as a nice sentence. They built it into furniture and food. In the langar, the free kitchen, everyone sits on the floor in the same rows, the pangat, and eats the same meal, whoever they are. Tradition tells that Guru Amar Das asked visitors, even the Mughal emperor Akbar, to eat in the langar before meeting him. Later, when Guru Gobind Singh created the Khalsa, the five who first stepped forward came from different castes and regions, and they drank amrit from one bowl. Sikhs will tell you honestly that caste didn't vanish from Punjabi life, and that the Gurus' teaching is still a challenge to their own communities too. But the rule on paper is clear, and it's short. Before you ask what someone's label is, see what's shining in them.
screen: `JOT — THE LIGHT IN EVERYONE.` · `JAAT — DON'T EVEN ASK.` · `ONE ROW, ONE MEAL: THE PANGAT.` · `FIVE CASTES, ONE BOWL.` · then, large: `SEE THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Picture someone you'll see today whom you usually file under a label: the new hire, the neighbor, the person at the counter, the relative you've decided about. Now set the label down, the way you'd set down a bag. Look at them again in your mind: a face, a life, a light. Breathe in, and silently say: see the light. Breathe out. Stay here a while. The bell holds the time.
Ask about the light. Guru Nanak's line in Asa: recognize the divine light in every person, and don't ask their caste.
Your line: see the light. Today, meet one person without the usual first question; let them be more than their label. Day two hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: In every gurdwara's langar, people of any background sit together in rows (pangat) on the floor and eat the same free meal; Sikh teaching rejects caste distinctions, though many Sikhs acknowledge caste still shapes parts of community life.

original.note: Gurmukhi: jot, light; jaanahu jot na poochhahu jaatee, recognize the light, don't ask the caste.

trapdoor: what you thought: caste just doesn't matter to God.
what it means: don't make someone's label the first thing you ask; recognize the light in them first.
what a scholar hears: Asa Mahala 1, Ang 349; jot (light) set against jaat (birth-group), with the imperative na poochhahu; the langar's pangat made the teaching physical.
